So. A business makes a certain amount of money from people paying for their services with taxed money. That income the business makes is then taxed. Then employees of the company are paid and the money is taxed once again. These employees then use this money to pay for services that are all taxed. The same money is taxed over and over again all the way down the line and around to the other side again. How can this manage to keep itself in existence? If our money is taxed over and over like this how can there really even be any money left over in the first place? And how would this all add up in terms of accountancy?

Stupid question: Something that I don't quite understand about taxation

Because tax money doesn't disappear from the economy, it is put back into the economy through payment of government employees, grants, purchase of goods and services from the private sector, etc. Taxes redistribute money, not destroy it.
Nice! Simple answer that explains exactly what I was wondering about that system. Seems obvious now. Thank you.

I think it is also important to note the economics of 'public goods' and how not everyone receives the same level of benefits. You can basically divide society into four groups. First, you have the people that use exactly their fair share of the public goods to which they are contributing via taxes. There are 'free riders' - people who don't pay at all and use public goods - who are essentially the homeless populations and those that avoid paying taxes. Then you have those that use more or less than what they pay.

It is also interesting to think about public goods and how much tax everyone pays. How often do you see CEOs and business executives playing on the swings in public parks? Not often (just my observation). However, these people are paying a higher proportion of the total cost of that park.

In general, public goods economics is a fascinating subject where most people just take as much as they want and have little to no regard for the rest of the agents in the economy.
